chunks: Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Abu Hamza who said:

Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) said to me: 'O Abu Hamza! Indeed, God cannot be described by limitation. Our Lord is too great to be described, so how can one who cannot be limited be described by limitation? Visions cannot comprehend Him, while He comprehends all visions, and He is al-Latif (the Subtle), al-Khabir (the All-Aware).'

key_terms.الأبصار: Visions, eyesights, perceptions — cannot encompass God (from Quran 6:103)
key_terms.اللَّطِيف: Al-Latif — one of the divine names; denotes subtlety, pervasiveness, imperceptibility, reaching the innermost
key_terms.الْخَبِير: Al-Khabir — one of the divine names; denotes all-awareness of manifest and hidden things
key_terms.مَحْدُودِيَّة: Limitation, finiteness — a quality that cannot be attributed to God
key_terms.يُحَدُّ: To be bounded, limited, defined by a limit (hadd); impossible for God

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Zayn al-Abidin say about describing God with limitation?
ai.summary: Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (Zayn al-Abidin, peace be upon him) teaches Abu Hamza al-Thumali — his close companion — that God transcends all limitation and description. The Imam grounds this teaching in the Quran (6:103): visions cannot encompass God, yet He encompasses all visions. This hadith reflects the Shia theological tradition of tanzih (divine transcendence), emphasizing that human categories and attributes cannot be applied to God. The audience, early Shia scholars and companions, would have understood this as a refutation of anthropomorphic theological positions circulating in early Islamic discourse.
